nodes.title: Paired comparison on the same items cancels item difficulty: variance falls from 1/6 to 1/9
nodes.body: The decision is whether candidate harness B beats incumbent A. Unpaired, the standard error is sqrt(Var(sA)+Var(sB))/sqrt(n), which is dominated by which tasks happened to be in the set, not by the difference being measured. Paired on the same items, Var(sA-sB) = Var_A + Var_B - 2Cov, so the shared component cancels; Miller (arXiv:2411.00640) computes for uniform item difficulties Var(x)=1/12 and correlation 0.5 that per-item variance falls from 1/6 to 1/9. Why this works: item difficulty enters both arms as the same additive term, so differencing annihilates it while the difference in treatment effect survives; this is variance reduction by design rather than by buying more samples, and it is the single cheapest lever available before any sequential machinery. Limitation: it requires the pairing structure to survive the intervention. If the candidate changes which items it can even attempt (a harness that spends fewer tokens and times out on hard items, or a scaffold that skips multi-file tasks), the covariance you get is not the covariance you assumed and pairing silently biases instead of tightening. Pairing also only answers a two-candidate question; a third candidate needs its own paired run.

nodes.title: 1 pp at sigma 1.5 pp needs 36 runs per arm; 2 pp needs 9 - Delta/sigma sets the sample size
nodes.body: Minimum sample size for a two-sample comparison is n >= 2((z_{alpha/2}+z_beta)/(Delta/sigma))^2 per arm. Bjarnason et al (arXiv:2602.07150) measured run-level SD of agentic pass@1 across 10 runs per configuration on 500 SWE-Bench-Verified tasks: sigma ranges about 0.7-1.8 pp, so a 2 pp improvement needs n=8-13 runs and a 1 pp improvement n=8-36. This is the arithmetic an accept-or-reject decision has to be built on: power depends on the non-centrality Delta/(sigma/sqrt(n)), and the formula is just its inversion at fixed alpha and 1-beta. Why this works: the quantity that matters is the delta expressed in units of run-to-run noise, so an eval that halves sigma halves the required runs at fixed effect size - which is why pairing and variance reduction beat adding tasks. Limitation: sigma-hat comes from roughly ten runs, so it is itself uncertain by a factor of several, and treating n=9 as sufficient when sigma-hat could be 40 percent low is the standard failure. The formula also assumes independent runs; repeated tasks (cluster by task) or shared prompt caching and serving batch inflate the true n, as Miller's clustered-SE ratios of up to 3.05 show.

nodes.title: Greedy decoding does not make an agent eval deterministic: SD stays above 1.5 pp at T=0
nodes.body: The folk fix for noisy comparisons is to set temperature 0 and assume the remaining delta is real. Two independent lines refute it. Bjarnason et al measured 60,000 trajectories (25.58B tokens, 1.88M tool calls, about 3,500 A100 hours) and found run-level SD of SWE-Bench pass@1 above 1.5 pp even at temperature 0; for Qwen3-32B on nano-agent it rose from 0.7 pp at T=0.6 to 1.2 pp at T=0.0, so variance did not decrease, it moved. The mechanism they document is first-token divergence: runs are byte-identical for tens of tokens, then split on one lexical choice (django__django-9296 diverges at token 94, search-the-Paginator-class versus check-the-source-code) and the two trajectories reach opposite pass/fail outcomes. Thinking Machines (He, 2025) supplies the deeper mechanism: the forward pass is run-to-run deterministic but not batch-invariant, because reduction order along the K dimension depends on batch size, so server load changes logits; 1000 greedy completions of one prompt gave 80 distinct outputs. Why this works as an explanation: it relocates the noise from sampling into kernel scheduling, which is why temperature cannot remove it. Limitation: batch-invariant kernels fix the serving-side component at about 1.6x latency (26s to 42s in their demo) but leave genuine tool-loop variance untouched, so sigma shrinks and never reaches zero.

nodes.title: Stopping at P(B>A)>0.95 is naive peeking; opportunity-loss stopping has FPR near 0.50
nodes.body: The rule everyone actually uses - watch the dashboard, ship when the posterior probability that B beats A passes gamma - is, under a flat prior, numerically identical to unadjusted repeated significance testing. Alpha is controlled at no level, and the realized false-positive rate depends on how often you looked, which is usually until you liked the answer. Schultzberg and Franberg (arXiv:2608.12949) sort methods into a three-tier hierarchy by which risk they control. Tier 1 is posterior coherence only: the expected-opportunity-loss rule of Stucchio (epsilon=0.02) sits here with FPR about 0.50, because it controls expected regret, not the chance of shipping a non-improvement. Tier 2 is Bayes-factor stopping at BF10 > 1/alpha, whose FPR under continuous monitoring is bounded by Ville's inequality. Tier 3 needs an empirical-Bayes prior over roughly 200 or more prior experiments per program to get per-metric FDR. The mechanism is that a Bayes factor is a nonnegative martingale with expectation 1 under the null, so Ville caps the probability its running maximum ever crosses a threshold, a time-uniform statement the fixed-n p-value cannot make. Limitation: Tier 3 calibration is defeated by winner-selected corpora, pooled programs or heterogeneous metrics regardless of corpus size, and Tier 1 rules are still what production dashboards implement.

nodes.title: Anytime validity is not inherently costly: induced sequential tests match fixed-N power
nodes.body: The folk theorem is that continuous monitoring forces a price - alpha spending, wider bounds, more samples - so you should pre-register one look. Koning and van Meer (arXiv:2501.03982) argue the price comes from a bad construction, not from optional stopping. For any valid fixed-N test they construct an induced anytime-valid sequential test that rejects by time N exactly when the fixed-N test would, hence with identical power, while remaining valid at every stopping time; they derive sequentialized z and t tests that coincide with the classical ones at N. Their motivating number: normal location, mu=0 versus mu=0.3, N=100, the fixed z-test rejects with probability 91 percent, while a plain SPRT tuned to a specific alternative rejects at some n<=N only 79 percent of the time. Why this works: the induced test's rejection region at each n is built from the fixed-N test at that n, so the fixed-N guarantee is recovered as a special case and validity at all stopping times follows from Ville's inequality by construction rather than by paying a penalty. Limitation: the guarantee is at N. An induced test is not optimized for deciding early, so if the real constraint is a third of the budget, the objective should be regret or expected stopping time and a Bayes-factor or SPRT rule with an explicit alternative is the better tool.

nodes.title: A Bayes-factor threshold is the only tier-2 rule bounding FPR under unlimited peeking
nodes.body: If the accept rule is stop when BF10 > 1/alpha, the false-positive rate under unlimited peeking is at most alpha, because under H0 the Bayes factor is a nonnegative martingale with expectation 1 and Ville's inequality caps the probability that its running maximum ever exceeds 1/alpha. That is a structurally different guarantee from a p-value: it holds at every stopping time, not at one pre-registered look. Schultzberg and Franberg further argue, via Arrow (1949) and Wald (1948), that for cost functions whose terminal payoff is affine in the posterior the Bayes-factor boundary is essentially optimal, making the frequentist versus Bayesian formulation largely a parameterization choice rather than a philosophical one. Why this works: a martingale plus a maximal inequality is exactly what converts a per-look statement into a statement about the whole path, and the BF is the likelihood ratio of the two hypotheses under comparison, so thresholds on it inherit the likelihood-ratio optimality structure. Limitation: the optimality class excludes nonlinear losses. If a false accept compounds - a broken harness accepted in round 3 corrupts the incumbent for rounds 4 through 20 - the loss is not affine in the posterior and no theorem covers the threshold; the rule stays valid but stops being efficient.

nodes.title: Selecting the best of m noisy candidates biases it up; the zoom correction adapts to the gap
nodes.body: The accept decision is usually keep whichever of m candidates scored highest, and reporting that winner's confidence interval unadjusted is invalid: the argmax is chosen on the same noise you are trying to average out, so E[max_i X_i] exceeds max_i E[X_i] and the gap grows with m and with how close the competitors are. Zrnic and Fithian (arXiv:2411.18569) introduce the zoom correction: form a simultaneous confidence region over all m candidates and project it onto the winning coordinate. Why this works: the region is built by inverting a zoom test whose acceptance radius is r_alpha OR Delta_j/2, where Delta_j is candidate j's suboptimality. Coordinates far from the top get a huge tolerance and consume almost no error budget, so power concentrates on the few genuinely competitive candidates and the effective multiplicity drops to the number of near-winners. That is why the interval approaches the uncorrected one when the winner is obvious and widens only when ten candidates tie, with no tuning parameter and no error-budget split. Limitation: it gives honest inference on the value of the winner you already selected, not a rule for selecting; and it requires a valid tail bound on the error vector, which in agent evals - clustered by task, heavy-tailed across runs - is precisely the hard part.

nodes.title: The Leaderboard Illusion: 27 private variants make a published rating a max over trials
nodes.body: This is the accept-or-reject failure as it actually occurs in the wild, documented. Chatbot Arena ratings are contaminated by selective disclosure: providers test private variants, observe the score, and release or retract accordingly, with 27 private Meta variants tested before the Llama-4 release. Sampling is also unequal - Google and OpenAI received an estimated 19.2 and 20.4 percent of all battles while 83 open-weight models shared 29.7 percent - and the paper estimates extra arena data is worth up to 112 percent relative gain on the arena distribution. Why this works as a distortion: the published rating is not the mean of a fixed design but the maximum over a hidden number of trials, so its bias is the winner's curse with m unknown and unbounded, and no per-model confidence interval can correct for trials that never appear in the data. The statistical defect is not noise, it is an unregistered search. Limitation, including of the paper's own remedy: the magnitudes are estimates from observables (battle counts, known variants), not a registry of private runs, so the bias is a bound under assumptions rather than a measured quantity; and no amount of better inference fixes it, because the missing input is how many candidates were tried, which only disclosure rules can supply.

nodes.title: Reusing one eval set for many decisions is adaptive analysis: it needs fresh data or noise
nodes.body: Every accept-or-reject decision taken on the same eval set changes what gets tested next: you keep the change that helped and discard the rest, so the sequence of looks is a sequence of adaptively chosen queries against fixed data. That is exactly the setting where a standard error computed as if the query had been fixed in advance stops being a bound. Dwork et al (arXiv:1411.2664) show the sample can survive exponentially many adaptively chosen expectation queries if the mechanism deliberately perturbs answers and coordinates them across queries, in the thresholdout style. Why this works: calibrated noise makes each answer insensitive to any single sample point, so the analyst's ability to select hypotheses that fit sample noise is bounded by a differential-privacy-style stability argument, and the bound composes over the whole adaptive sequence rather than per query. Two cheaper substitutes dominate practice - a holdout touched once per decision, and pre-registration of the item set, alpha and stopping rule before the run. Limitation: the DP guarantees are worst-case and loose at realistic eval sizes, and the perturbation is often unacceptable when the effect to detect is 1-2 pp; Kapoor et al (arXiv:2407.01502) document that agent benchmarks frequently have no holdout at all, so in practice the failure is not mitigated, only unrecognized.

nodes.title: Below a few hundred items CLT intervals under-cover; AIME has 15 problems and LiveBench 55
nodes.body: Bowyer, Aitchison and Ivanova (arXiv:2503.01747) simulated 100 theta values times 200 datasets times N in {3,10,30,100}, 80,000 eval datasets, and checked coverage at 100 nominal levels from 0.8 to 0.995. CLT intervals under-cover badly at small N, bootstrap also under-covers systematically, and Bayesian credible intervals track nominal. The motivating sizes are the sizes people actually use for hard tasks: CUAD 510 documents, FrontierMath about 300 problems with some categories under 3, AIME 15 problems, SWE-bench Verified 500, MLE-bench 75, LiveBench about 55 examples per task. Why this works: the CLT's error is O(1/sqrt(N)) with a skew-dependent constant, and for a bounded, highly skewed per-item score that constant is large exactly in the regime of small N; a Bayesian interval integrates the likelihood under a stated prior instead of asserting normality, so its coverage error is governed by prior sensitivity rather than by N. Limitation: this fixes coverage for a single mean. The paper is explicit that no prior rescues a wrong likelihood, and the prior is itself an unvalidated degree of freedom on benchmarks this small; a comparative claim such as harness A beats B on this 40-task subset still needs the paired or hierarchical machinery, not a credible interval per arm.

nodes.title: A low-rank task-by-model matrix borrows strength; debiased one-step CIs hit the bound
nodes.body: With m candidates and T tasks you do not have m times T independent experiments: ability correlates across tasks and across models. Li et al (arXiv:2605.29395) model the task-by-model ability matrix Theta* as low rank, estimate it with a debiased one-step estimator plus cross-fitting, and obtain asymptotically valid intervals attaining the semiparametric efficiency bound, together with simultaneous confidence sets for per-task ranks and top-K via Gaussian and multiplier bootstrap. Why this works: low rank asserts that a handful of latent factors explain most of the task-by-model table, so each cell is estimated from its own sparse data plus the factor structure shared with every other cell - the effective sample size per cell rises - and the one-step debiasing removes the regularization bias that would otherwise invalidate the interval. The paper reports the largest gains in the sparse regime, which is exactly the regime of a specialized agent benchmark with a few hundred tasks. Limitation: the rank must be chosen, under-ranking biases every interval and over-ranking returns the noise you pooled to escape; and the guarantee is about the population ranking over a task distribution, not about the single repository an RSI loop is editing, where the task population is one repo's issue tracker.

nodes.title: IRT picks 100 of 14,000 MMLU items, yet item analysis alone did not cut variance
nodes.body: Selective evaluation is the cheapest variance lever available: tinyBenchmarks (arXiv:2402.14992) selects about 100 curated MMLU items whose IRT parameters span the difficulty range and recovers full-benchmark accuracy. Why this works: items differ enormously in information. An item every model gets right, or no model gets right, contributes nothing to distinguishing abilities, while a mid-difficulty item does, so choosing items by Fisher information buys the same estimate at a fraction of the cost. But Madaan et al (arXiv:2406.10229), testing whether IRT and item-analysis reduce variance directly, report that these techniques struggle to meaningfully reduce variance for comparison, while a different trick, reframing multiple-choice as completion, did help models around 7B. The reconciliation is that item information is defined for estimating one ability level, whereas a paired accept-or-reject decision needs the per-item difference: items where both arms are right or both wrong carry zero signal regardless of IRT difficulty. Limitation: item parameters are estimated from a model population that must contain the candidate, and a harness change that shifts the difficulty curve - longer tool loops, a different token budget - breaks calibration; a 100-item proxy tuned for leaderboard-scale gaps is not calibrated for the 1-2 pp deltas a loop decides on.

nodes.title: A stationary-optimal accept rule stops tracking after change; windowed statistics keep up
nodes.body: An RSI loop is non-stationary by construction: the harness changes, the checkpoint changes, the repo accumulates patches. A rule that pools all history to estimate sigma and the incumbent mean is answering a question about a system that no longer exists. Garivier and Moulines (arXiv:0805.3415) formalize the abruptly changing bandit: policies optimal under stationarity fail to track the best arm after a change point, and discounted-UCB and sliding-window-UCB variants achieve regret matching a lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Why this works: the window bounds the age of data entering each estimate, so it trades variance (fewer effective samples) against bias (a stale mean), and under abrupt change the bias term dominates the variance term once the window passes the change point - the discount factor is the continuous analogue of the same trade. Limitation: the window length is a hyperparameter whose optimum depends on an unknown change rate, and shortening it inflates the n that the paired and MDE arithmetic demands, so non-stationarity and statistical power are in direct conflict with no free setting. No published work measures the change rate of an agent harness, so the window cannot be derived, only guessed.

nodes.title: Six leaderboard metrics behave like 1.7 independent axes, so multiplicity costs less power
nodes.body: Sequential and simultaneous corrections are parameterized by k comparisons, but that k is nominal. Sha and Zhao (arXiv:2603.29357) estimate Effective Dimensionality as the participation ratio of the centered benchmark-score spectrum: the Open LLM Leaderboard's 6 scores come out at ED=1.7, and BBH versus MMLU-Pro correlate at rho=0.96, with breadth varying more than 20x across benchmarks. Why this works as an argument about decisions: if the metrics are nearly collinear, testing all six is close to testing twice, so a Bonferroni or alpha-spending correction over six is conservative and the power lost to correcting is small - good news for the sequential machinery above. The same fact is bad news for the accept decision itself: a candidate that moves one axis moves its clones, so a win on 5 of 6 benchmarks is closer to one win than five, and the evidence for a real improvement is weaker than the count of green cells suggests. Limitation: ED is estimated across a model population and a fixed metric set, so it is not a per-decision quantity; a harness change that pushes the candidate off the population manifold makes the estimated ED, and the correction inferred from it, wrong in exactly the case the loop cares about.

nodes.title: Horizon: success collapses within a few actions, not exponentially (36.3% of 3,132 trajectories)
nodes.body: The HORIZON benchmark holds horizon as the controlled variable across Web/WebArena, OS/AgentBench, DB/MAC-SQL and embodied IsaacSim, scoring 3,132 trajectories (1,995 failures, 1,137 successes, 36.3% overall; Web 24.1%, OS 40.3%, DB 36.9%, Embodied 42.2%). The curve is not the smooth geometric decay predicted when each subgoal succeeds independently at rate p: the data show a sharp transition region inside a handful of actions, then near-floor success. The paper separates intrinsic horizon H* (minimum effective actions an optimal policy needs) from compositional depth s (longest chain of decision nodes on any path). The mechanism is state coupling: a wrong decision at action k changes the state actions k+1..n operate on, so failure is conditional on the prefix, and depth rather than step count governs reliability. Embodied runs show the shape: GPT-5 at 0.926 -> 0.407 -> 0.259 -> 0.074, Claude-4 at 0.963 -> 0.259 -> 0.111 -> 0.037 across four depth levels. Honest limitation: the breaking point is a transition band, not a threshold, is model- and domain-conditional, and no empirically validated theory derives it from task structure.

nodes.title: Context bloat is 47.9-55.7% of terminal failures and 56.6-65.1% of triggers in a 72h loop
nodes.body: The Endurance Wall study simulates a production harness for 72 hours at 12 tasks/hour (864 tasks/run, 100 seeds/cell, 20k starting context growing 6k tokens/hour to a 100k cap) and scores every task with an independent verifier. Two structural facts dominate the baseline taxonomy: context bloat is the top terminal class at every hazard level (47.9%, 52.9%, 55.7%) and the top trigger of any failure (56.6-65.1% of triggers), with skill misroute 12.8-13.3%, starvation 10.9-12.1% and silent no-op 9.4-10.0% roughly stable. Why this works as a diagnosis: it identifies the failure as endogenous, i.e. the loop's own accumulated transcript is a load-bearing input that degrades with age, so remedies must operate on the transcript (compaction) rather than on the task stream. Honest limitation and scope warning: the hazard grid is declared, not fitted to telemetry, and the whole result is a discrete-event simulator of one frozen task stream and one model tier; the authors themselves say the level values are not a production night's numbers, only the intervention ranking is meant to survive re-anchoring.

nodes.title: A failed task lifts the next failure rate by +1.51/+3.72/+14.22pp across hazard levels
nodes.body: The measurable signature of compounding is the conditional gap Delta_comp = P(task t fails | task t-1 fails) - P(task t fails | task t-1 verified OK). Baseline values are +1.51pp (low hazard), +3.72pp (mid), +14.22pp (high); at high hazard the post-failure failure rate is 0.401 against 0.259 after a verified success. Why this works as a measurement: it isolates contamination from base rate, because both arms of the contrast share the same task stream and model tier, so the difference can only come from what the previous task left behind (a poisoned transcript, a half-edited repo, a wrong assumption carried forward). The mechanism is state carryover: the loop's persistent context and working tree are shared mutable state, so one unrecovered error raises the cost of every subsequent decision until something resets the channel. Honest limitation: Delta_comp is correlational and simulator-derived; a common cause (e.g. a hard stretch of tasks) would inflate it, and the study only partially controls for task difficulty by freezing a single stream. The high-hazard value is also the most fragile to the declared hazard grid.

nodes.title: Compaction restores failure independence (gap to +0.24pp) and pays for itself at 3.4-4.2x QPD
nodes.body: Periodic context compaction every 6 hours (summarize and rewrite the transcript at 0.5x token cost) cuts bloat from 55.7% to 2.4% of terminal failures, drops retry-ladder exhaustions from 1.55 per run to 0.00, and shrinks Delta_comp from +1.51/+3.72/+14.22pp to +0.24/+0.88/+1.48pp, going slightly negative (-0.29/-0.56/+0.17pp) in arms that combine it with veto. A negative gap means the task after a failure succeeds more often than the task after a success, i.e. a repair effect. The mechanism is that amplification is mediated by the transcript, and compaction is the one intervention that removes the mediator rather than masking it, so failures become approximately independent samples again and a retry has a real chance of a different outcome. Honest limitation: compaction alone buys almost no endurance at high hazard (+0.27h) because the residual mix then shifts to skill misroute (33.0%), starvation (28.1%) and silent no-op (23.9%), which compaction cannot touch; and a summary is lossy, so the mechanism trades contamination for information loss whose rate this study does not measure.

nodes.title: Checkpoint-restart buys 3.5-8.1h but inflates the apparent-vs-verified gap from 2.9 to 21.9pp
nodes.body: Snapshotting state every 2 hours and restarting from the last good snapshot when the retry ladder is exhausted (3 attempts, 50% each, 3,000 tokens per restart) looks like the classic 'restart from clean state' remedy. It does add endurance (+3.5/+6.5/+8.1 hours) but drops quality-per-dollar below parity (0.92/0.86/0.80x) and, the sharper finding, inflates the gap between self-declared completion and independently verified success from a 0.7-2.9pp baseline to 9.0/15.1/21.9pp. The mechanism is that re-execution from a snapshot re-runs the task against the same un-fixed environment and the same un-fixed plan, so the residual error is silently re-absorbed and the run is recorded as complete; the restart resets the context counter but not the cause, and it re-inflates context from the snapshot so bloat returns to 65.3%. Why this matters for any RSI loop: a checkpointed loop reports more success the less it deserves, which corrupts the very signal a self-improving loop trains on. Honest limitation: the simulator's verifier is deterministic and mechanical, so these exact gaps depend on verifier coverage; a verifier with its own error rate would move them, and the study is explicit that this is one frozen tier and stream.

nodes.title: Low-confidence veto buys 8.7-13.5h at QPD ~1.0x without narrowing amplification (15.31pp)
nodes.body: Vetoing results whose confidence falls below a threshold, at 500 tokens per veto, is the only single intervention whose endurance gain grows with hazard while holding cost parity (QPD 0.98-1.02x), and compact+veto is the cheapest crossing of the wall: +35.5h at high hazard, 72h success 0.945, QPD 3.91x, integrity cost 0.31pp. The mechanism is economic rather than epistemic: the veto does not reduce Delta_comp (it actually widens to +15.31pp) and it increases cascade exhaustions (1.55 -> 1.67), because it defers work rather than fixing it. What it does is intercept before contamination at a fixed low price, and as hazard rises more results fall below threshold, so the number of intercepts, and therefore the total hours saved, grows. Why this works: it converts an unbounded downstream cost into a bounded per-event cost, which is exactly the right shape when you cannot tell which output is wrong but you can tell which output is uncertain. Honest limitation: the confidence signal is assumed calibrated, and no calibration measurement is reported; on a miscalibrated model veto becomes random rejection with the same token price and no endurance gain.

nodes.title: Continuous oracle state lifts success 19-38%, and its lead widens from 7% to 18% as runs lengthen
nodes.body: The oracle-state intervention replaces a failing agent's accumulated history with ground-truth structured state, which lets one separate 'the agent lacked the facts' from 'the agent had the facts and still failed'. Replacing context only after failure recovers under 10% of 420 failed WebArena trajectories, but maintaining oracle state throughout the trajectory improves success by 19-38%, and the gap between oracle-maintained and self-generated state grows from 7% to 18% as trajectories lengthen. The mechanism is that the deficit is not retrievability but maintenance: a correct fact inserted once decays in influence as the transcript grows, so the benefit scales with how continuously the state is re-asserted, not with how much context is available at any single step. Why this works as a causal test rather than a correlation: the intervention changes only the state, holding the policy and tools fixed, so the improvement is attributable to state quality alone. Honest limitation: oracle state is not deployable (it is a diagnostic upper bound), the study covers WebArena only with two models (Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.2), and 'structured state' was hand-built for that environment.

nodes.title: Context explains 11.7% of failures; 58-74% persist after context and environment are restored
nodes.body: This is the most direct test of the assumption behind most long-horizon engineering (compress, filter, restructure history). In 420 failed WebArena trajectories across two models, human annotators attribute only 11.7% of failures to context-caused errors, post-hoc context replacement recovers under 10%, and 58-74% of failures survive restoring both context and environment. The convergence of an intervention-based estimate with an independent human-attribution estimate is what makes this credible: two methods with different biases land on the same minority share. The mechanism is that many failures are planning or execution errors already committed to state the agent cannot re-derive, so no history repair rescues them; repair must happen at the decision, not at the transcript. Why this works as evidence: it predicts that context engineering alone hits a ceiling and that subgoal-level verification is the higher-yield lever, consistent with continuous oracle state helping while post-hoc repair does not. Honest limitation: WebArena is a bounded web environment, two models, and the oracle upper bound is not deployable; 'context' was operationalized as accumulated history, which may understate slower contamination.

nodes.title: All 18 models degrade as input grows; shuffled haystacks beat coherent ones for every model
nodes.body: Chroma's Context Rot holds task complexity fixed and varies only input length across ~194,480 calls on 18 models (Claude Opus/Sonnet 4, GPT-4.1 family, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3). Performance falls with length on every model even for needle retrieval and repeated-word copying; one distractor hurts and four compound, amplified at longer lengths; lower needle-question semantic similarity degrades faster. The counterintuitive result is that logically shuffled, locally incoherent haystacks beat coherent ones across all 18 models. The mechanism is attention competition: coherent text creates strong local associations that compete with the queried item, so well-organized context is not automatically easier to use. Why this matters here: the degradation is a property of input processing, not only of task difficulty, so a long run degrades even when nothing goes wrong. Honest limitation, stated by the authors: they do not explain the mechanism behind the degradation, and near-perfect needle-in-a-haystack scores mask the effect because retrieval is not reasoning over context; the attention-structure account remains an unproven hypothesis.

nodes.title: Intrinsic self-correction adds no information and can lower accuracy; verification must be external
nodes.body: The ICLR 2024 result is blunt: without external feedback, asking a model to review and correct its own reasoning does not reliably improve accuracy and sometimes degrades it. Why this works as an explanation: self-correction conditioned only on the model's own prior output is a re-sample from the same posterior, so it cannot import the information that would distinguish a wrong answer from a right one; the model's confidence is unchanged, so the error is stable under reflection. The consequence for long-horizon design is structural: a 'reflect and retry' loop has no mechanism to break an error chain, whereas a mechanical check (test suite, schema validation, state diff, independent verifier) introduces new information and can. This is the same logic that makes the veto arm work only if the confidence signal is genuinely external, and the same reason checkpointing fails in the endurance study when the verifier is inside the loop. Honest limitation: the finding is scoped to reasoning benchmarks and intrinsic self-correction; with a tool that returns real feedback, the loop is no longer intrinsic, and how much external feedback is enough before an agent can safely self-correct is not established.

nodes.title: Multi-turn runs lose 39% versus single-turn through premature commitment, not lost aptitude
nodes.body: Across 200,000+ simulated conversations, 6 generation tasks and all top open and closed models, multi-turn performance drops 39% on average against the single-turn baseline with identical information. The decomposition matters more than the headline: aptitude falls only slightly, while variance and unreliability rise sharply. The mechanism the authors identify is premature commitment: models make assumptions in early turns, commit to a final solution, then over-rely on that commitment, so a wrong early turn is not corrected later, it is built upon. This is why the failure looks like drift rather than decay: the model is not getting worse at the task, it is executing a plan whose premises stopped being true. Why this works as an explanation of long-run degradation: it predicts that intervening on the plan (replanning, subgoal checks) beats intervening on the words (re-prompting, asking it to reconsider), and it predicts that a fresh context with an explicit state summary should outperform a long faithful transcript, which is what the harness write-ups and the oracle-state result both show. Honest limitation: simulated user turns, generation tasks, and the effect size is a single average over heterogeneous task families.

nodes.title: pass^k exposes a reliability ceiling: 75% per trial is only 42% pass^3; tau-bench pass^8 <25%
nodes.body: pass^k requires all k independent trials to succeed (C(c,k)/C(n,k)), unlike pass@k which credits any success. In tau-bench, gpt-4o solves under 50% of tasks and pass^8 drops below 25% in retail; a model at 75% per trial is at roughly 42% for pass^3 under independence, and far lower if trials are correlated. The mechanism is that per-trial success hides the tail of the distribution, and long-horizon work is a tail problem: an unattended loop is effectively asking for a long conjunction of successes, so the relevant statistic is the conjunction rate, not the mean. Why this works as a reporting fix: it makes variance visible and forces the question 'how often does this whole run succeed unattended', which is the operational question. Honest limitation: pass^k assumes exchangeable trials, and real harnesses are not exchangeable (state accumulates across tasks), which is exactly what Delta_comp measures; pass^k therefore understates the compounding penalty of a continuous loop and is a floor, not an estimate.

nodes.title: A feature-list harness with progress log and clean end state defeats premature completion
nodes.body: The practitioner harness for multi-session coding agents has two parts. An initializer session writes init.sh (how to run the app), a claude-progress.txt log, an initial git commit, and feature_list.json enumerating every end-to-end feature marked passes:false (200+ for a claude.ai clone); JSON is chosen over Markdown because models are less likely to inappropriately edit or delete structured entries. Each later session reads pwd, the progress file, the feature list and git log, implements exactly one feature, commits descriptively, and must end in a clean state (mergeable, no major bugs, documented). Named failure modes: one-shotting the app until context runs out mid-implementation, leaving an undocumented half-feature for the next session to guess at (stated to happen even with compaction, which does not always pass clear instructions forward), and premature completion, where a later instance surveys progress and declares the job done. The mechanism is externalized enumerable ground truth: an un-checked item is a falsifiable claim about remaining work, so the agent cannot satisfy the state by self-assessment. Honest limitation: an engineering write-up with no controlled numbers, no baseline, no failure rates, and the primary page was unreachable during this research, so detail comes from mirrors.

nodes.title: Horizon is measured by four incompatible proxies, so published decay curves cannot compose
nodes.body: The Horizon Gap survey reads 1,547 arXiv papers from 2024-2026 through a six-category frame (planning, memory, execution, training, evaluation, foundations) crossed with where horizon is carried: within-context, within-task-beyond-context, cross-task-persistent. Its sharpest methodological finding is that long-horizon is operationalized by at least four non-equivalent proxies, so a 50-step run, a 2-hour run and a 100k-token run are all called long-horizon while stressing different mechanisms; its central substantive finding is that outcome-only rewards grow uninformative as horizons lengthen, which is why the field manufactures step-level signals (process reward models, credit assignment, trajectory diagnostics). The mechanism is measurement drift: when the independent variable is whatever the harness happens to count, results do not accumulate and one symptom gets four incompatible explanations. Why this is load-bearing: it is how one paper finds collapse and another finds smooth decay without either being wrong. Honest limitation: the survey's own filter is disclosed as 26.8% bleed, and it concludes that no general empirically validated theory of long-horizon degradation exists, only partially contradictory phenomena.

nodes.title: Users approve 97% of per-action permission prompts but reject 39% of plan approvals
nodes.body: Problem: agent systems place a human at every action gate and count the gate as oversight. Hard part: the gate's throughput is human attention, and a decision made 200 times a day degrades into a keypress. Anthropic's auto-mode rollout data (Aug 2026, updated 22 Oct 2026) shows the asymmetry: 97% of individual permission prompts are approved (3% rejected) while 39% of plan-approval dialogues are rejected. The mechanism is scope: a plan dialogue asks for one judgment over a whole trajectory with intent stated, so there is something to disagree with; a single tool call is too small to evaluate on its merits, so the cheapest response wins. Corroborating behavior: 49.5% of active CLI users have hand-written a Bash allow-rule (43% interpreter rules like Bash(python:*) that amount to arbitrary code execution), 62% have used bypassPermissions or 'don't ask again', and 25% of interactive sessions start in bypass mode - the gate is routed around rather than used. Limitation: these are logged production rates, not a measure of attention; the 97% is not conditioned on prompt difficulty, so it cannot separate 'prompts were mostly fine' from 'users stopped reading'.

nodes.title: Humans caught 13.6% of swapped-in dangerous commands while the classifier blocked 89%
nodes.body: Anthropic ran a controlled test with 1,053 paid testers in which one permission prompt was replaced by a clearly dangerous command. Humans caught 143/1,053 = 13.6%; the auto-mode classifier blocked 89% (937/1,053). Head to head, auto blocked 800 commands humans had approved, and humans blocked 6 that auto allowed. Human block rate fell from about 17% early in a session to about 5% after 50 or more prior prompts, while the classifier stayed flat. The mechanism is base-rate training of vigilance: a stream of benign approvals moves the reviewer's prior toward 'approve', and the cost of reading is paid on every decision while the benefit is realized rarely, so effort decays with repetition - the classifier has no such channel because it re-evaluates each input identically. Limitation: only the prompt text was swapped, so nothing dangerous could actually run; the attacks are synthetic rather than real traffic; and the 13.6% is best read as a lower bound on miss rates under engineered fatigue, not an estimate of field performance.

nodes.title: Escalating every action is not safest: danger-through is 69% at full escalation vs 56% at 64%
nodes.body: Problem: deciding which agent actions to stop, when the human reviewer is a depleting resource. Hard part: reviewer reliability is endogenous to the escalation load the policy itself creates. Turan (arXiv:2606.08919) models reviewer reliability as r(l) = max(0.2, 1 - 0.02*max(0, l - C)) where l is escalations and C is capacity: past capacity, reliability collapses toward 0.2, so extra escalations add queue depth without adding scrutiny. Realized danger-through is therefore inverted-U in escalation rate, with safety optima strictly below full escalation: C=10 gives 64% escalation and 56% danger vs 69% at 100%; C=25 gives 64%/42% vs 57%; C=50 gives 72%/22% vs 39%. Why this works: the curve is a queueing effect, not a psychology claim - if inspection is throughput-limited, a longer queue is inspected more shallowly per item, so the marginal escalation can have negative safety value. Limitation: r(l) is simulated with chosen constants (slope 0.02, floor 0.2, reviewer never errs when fresh), so only the shape is claimed and absolute numbers are lower bounds; no human was measured anywhere in the paper.

nodes.title: Flooding with 50 filler escalations raised attack success to 40% against an 88%-escalating guard
nodes.body: Same paper, adversarial variant. The attack: submit many routine actions for escalation so the reviewer's queue saturates, then submit the harmful one. A guard that escalates 88% of actions reaches 40% attack success at only k=50 filler actions, with a ceiling near 80%. A load-aware guard that escalates 26% holds attack success at 0% until roughly 100 fillers, reaches about 10% by k=110, and only approaches its ceiling around k=250. The mechanism is that the attacker never has to defeat the classifier - only to exhaust the shared human capacity that the classifier routes into - so attention itself becomes the exploitable surface, and flooding is cheaper than fooling. Why this works: capacity is finite and common across all actions, letting an adversary manipulate the denominator of reviewer reliability without touching the numerator. Limitation: simulated reviewer, one 125-action dataset, and an attacker assumed to know the escalation policy; no live system has had its flooding behavior measured, so the k=50 threshold is illustrative rather than predictive.

nodes.title: Three reviewer personas agreed on which agent actions are risky at only Fleiss kappa=0.52
nodes.body: Turan had 125 agent actions hand-labeled by three LLM reviewer personas standing in for humans. Agreement was moderate: Fleiss kappa 0.52, with pairwise Cohen kappa 0.42 (cautious vs pragmatic), 0.47 (pragmatic vs compliance), 0.71 (cautious vs compliance). The pragmatic persona called 87 actions safe where the cautious one called 45; the majority label matched the author's gold label 74% of the time. The mechanism is that 'risky' is a threshold on a cost tradeoff rather than a property, and reviewers holding different cost ratios will disagree without either being wrong - which is why accuracy is the wrong metric and risk-coverage curves, AURC and Neyman-Pearson operating points are the right ones. Why this works as an argument: if disagreement is policy divergence rather than error, then a guard must be calibrated to a declared cost matrix, and no amount of labeling effort yields a single ground truth. Limitation: the personas are LLM proxies, all five results rest on one 125-item dataset, and the gold labels are the author's own - so kappa=0.52 measures the difficulty of the labeling task, not human inter-rater agreement.

nodes.title: Learning-to-defer with workload constraints cut misclassification cost 8.4% over static-human L2D
nodes.body: Two lines of work make reviewer capacity a first-class constraint rather than a post-hoc filter. DeCCaF (Alves et al., arXiv:2403.06906) does cost-sensitive deferral with per-expert work-capacity limits solved by constraint programming, requiring only one expert prediction per instance, and reports an average 8.4% reduction in misclassification cost over baselines with 9 synthetic fraud analysts. FALCON (arXiv:2604.00904) puts psychologically grounded fatigue curves into a constrained MDP whose state is task features plus cumulative human workload, trained with PPO-Lagrangian under a cooperation budget, and ships the FA-L2D benchmark that sweeps fatigue from near-static to rapidly degrading; it beats prior L2D across coverage and generalizes zero-shot to unseen experts. The mechanism is that when reviewer accuracy is a function of cumulative load, routing becomes a sequential resource-allocation problem, and greedy per-item deferral is not optimal - the policy must learn to spend scarce review where it changes the outcome. Limitation: both evaluate against synthetic or modeled experts; nobody has measured the fatigue curve on real reviewers, so the reported gains are conditional on an assumed curve and may not survive contact with real attention.

nodes.title: Maintainers merge 24.2 pp fewer AI PRs than the SWE-bench grader accepts, and rate horizons ~7x shorter
nodes.body: METR (note 2026-03-10) had 4 active maintainers (scikit-learn, Sphinx, pytest; 3 of 12 repos, 95 of 500 issues) review 296 AI-generated PRs plus 47 golden human patches, blinded, inside real GitHub, paid hourly with a quality bonus. Their merge decisions average 24.2 pp (SE 2.7) below the automated SWE-bench grader, so roughly half of test-passing PRs would not be merged. Rejection reasons in order: code quality, other, breaks other code, core functionality failure, failing grader. On the time-horizon framing, Claude Sonnet 4.5 reads as a ~50-minute task horizon by the grader and ~8 minutes by these maintainers. The mechanism is that the grader measures 'does the stated test pass' while the maintainer measures 'will this cost more than it saves over the repo's lifetime' - a maintenance-cost judgment that no test encodes, which is exactly the part that requires human attention and cannot be graded away. Limitation: one benchmark subset, one harness, one shot per PR (no iteration), no CI for reviewers; the 9.6 pp/yr closing trend is p<0.10 and marked fragile, so this is a snapshot, not a law.

nodes.title: Only 68% of real merged human patches re-merged, so a review rate needs a paired baseline
nodes.body: In the same METR study, the 47 golden patches were real human patches already merged into those repos. These maintainers re-merged only 68% of them, while rating 85% as achieving at least 80% of the task - so even 'known-good' work fails a re-review a third of the time. The mechanism is that an absolute merge rate confounds patch quality with reviewer strictness and with lab-versus-real context; normalizing to a golden baseline subtracts the person rather than the task, which is why paired designs beat between-subject ones. Why this works: the baseline absorbs the reviewer-specific offset, turning an uninterpretable score into a ratio that can be compared across reviewers, models and time. Limitation: the golden set is 47 patches judged by the same 4 maintainers, so the 68% ceiling is itself a small-sample estimate; it also silently redefines 'correct' as 'what these four would do', and any reported accuracy above 68% is measuring agreement with a person rather than with truth.

nodes.title: Labelling code as LLM-generated raised fixation time up to 60% without raising thoroughness
nodes.body: Khojah et al. (ASE 2026, arXiv:2606.26505) ran an eye-tracking wizard-of-Oz study: 32 practitioners from 20 organizations, 7.0 +/- 5.1 years experience, reviewing 4 PRs of about 77 +/- 10 LoC with faults and smells injected. All code was actually pre-October-2021 human code, but some regions were labelled 'CodeForgeAI' with a timestamp and prompt. Saccade length - their thoroughness proxy - did not change; fixation time on the LLM-labelled regions rose by up to 60% for more complex code. 20 of 32 said their evaluation criteria were unchanged; 12 applied different criteria; 14 used the prompt itself as requirement context. The mechanism is that provenance is a salience cue that reallocates a fixed attention budget rather than expanding it: reviewers stare longer at regions they distrust while reading no more broadly, so a label buys scrutiny of the suspected part at the cost of the rest. Limitation: n=32 within-subject lab task, 10 minutes per PR, no tests supplied, correctness not scored - it measures gaze, not defects, so 'more fixation' must not be read as 'more errors caught'.

nodes.title: Independent human-AI aggregation beat AI-as-advisor 4.45 pp at a 22-49% tiebreak cost
nodes.body: Berger et al. (arXiv:2603.29866) test a hybrid confirmation tree: human and AI judge independently, agreement is accepted, disagreement goes to a second human tiebreaker. Across 10 datasets, more than 41,000 human judgments, 1,229 decision-makers and 3,220 cases (dermoscopy, colonoscopy, sentiment, deception, deepfake, rearrest), the tree beat AI-as-advisor in all 10, +0.2 to +6.6 pp, pooled +4.45 pp (95% HDI 3.73-5.27). With XAI explanations across 16 conditions and 50,390 decisions it was better in 11, similar in 2, worse in 3 - all three where humans were at chance. Gains were +8 pp for low performers, +3.2 mid, +1.9 high. The mechanism is signal detection: people cannot discriminate correct from incorrect AI advice well enough to adjudicate it, so showing advice first destroys the independent signal, and preserving independence yields two noisy estimates that combine well. Limitation: a re-analysis of existing datasets with no live deployment, and the accuracy gain is explicitly bought with extra human judgments in 22% to 49% of cases - in a capacity-constrained system that tiebreak load may cost more than the 4.45 pp is worth.

nodes.title: 26.6% of erroneous ECG interpretations went uncorrected by clinicians (95% CI 6.4-65.6%)
nodes.body: A 2026 npj Digital Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis of human oversight of clinical AI, as summarized in a secondary source, pooled four heterogeneous real-world studies of computerized ECG interpretation: 26.6% of erroneous interpretations were not recognized or corrected, with a 95% CI of 6.4% to 65.6%. A separate pooling of three adjusted cohorts found clinicians had about 10 times higher odds of being correct when the advice was correct than when it was incorrect (OR 10.19, 95% CI 7.43-13.98). The mechanism is prior-shifting: the advice converts an independent derivation task into a confirmation task, so when the advice is wrong the reviewer must overcome both the shifted prior and the authority cue, precisely when the case looks most routine. Why this works as a measurement: error-interception rate measures what oversight is supposed to do, whereas agreement rate rises even when the human has been captured. Limitation: the review mixes decades of computerized decision support with modern AI and could not pool LLM-era studies for heterogeneity - and I read a secondary summary, not the primary paper, so treat 26.6% as a warning signal with a nearly uninformative interval rather than a rate.

nodes.title: Asynchronous monitoring reached 6% false-negative at 1% false-positive with zero runtime latency
nodes.body: Stickland et al. (arXiv:2512.13526) study asynchronous control: a monitor reviews agent actions after the fact instead of gating them, so no runtime latency is imposed while still attempting to disrupt attacks before irreversible harm. They build 5 software-engineering environments and run an adversarial blue-team/red-team game, ending with an ensemble monitor at 6% false-negative rate at 1% false-positive on a held-out environment, then extrapolate deployment risk from that FNR with an explicit model, sensitivity analysis and stated invalidity conditions. The mechanism is that the scarce resource is not only human time but the agent's throughput: moving review off the critical path converts a blocking interrupt into a queued item, and a queue can be triaged asynchronously while the agent keeps working. Why this works: latency and oversight are decoupled, so oversight is paid for in reaction time rather than in agent stalls. Limitation: it applies only to harms that are not yet irreversible when detected; the extrapolation rests on assumptions the authors say they cannot validate; and the monitor is a model, not a human, so this is an alternative to human attention rather than a measurement of it.

nodes.title: Interrupted work finished faster with no quality loss but at higher stress and effort
nodes.body: Mark, Gudith and Klocke (CHI 2008, doi 10.1145/1357054.1357072) interrupted participants mid-task: interrupted tasks were completed faster than uninterrupted ones with no quality difference, but at measurably higher stress, frustration, time pressure and effort; the context of the interruption did not matter, and personality traits such as openness and personal structure predicted disruption cost. The mechanism is compensatory speed: people absorb an interruption by working faster afterwards, so the cost is invisible in completion time and product quality and surfaces instead as workload - which is why interrupt cost must be measured in stress, effort, or error rate at a fixed pace, never in duration. Why this works as a design constraint: a system that instruments only latency will systematically under-price interruptions and over-schedule them, and that error is invisible in exactly the metrics such systems collect. Limitation: the widely repeated '23 minutes to resume' figure comes from Mark's separate observational work and does not appear in this paper - I could not verify it in primary text, so treat 23 minutes as unverified; the study is also a lab task with student-age participants, not code review.

nodes.title: Only 14% of code-review comments concern defects; median Google change is 24 lines
nodes.body: Bacchelli and Bird (ICSE 2013, Microsoft, 200 reviews and 570 comments) found that although defect finding motivates review, only 14% of review outcomes and comments were about defects, with 65 logical issues and the remainder design, style, and knowledge transfer. Sadowski et al. (ICSE-SEIP 2018) describe Google at scale: about 20,000 changes per day, a median change of 24 lines, about 90% touching fewer than 10 files, a median of 1 approver with under 25% having more than one, median time-to-approval under 4 hours and over 80% of reviews finishing in a single round. The mechanism is that a review decision is cheap when the diff is small and the number of rounds is one: decision cost scales with the number of independent things a reviewer must hold at once, so small changes plus a single approver is what keeps a 20k/day queue moving. Limitation: these are descriptive medians at one company on human-written changes; the 14% defect share counts comments and therefore undercounts implicit defect prevention; and none of it transfers cleanly to agent diffs, which arrive faster, larger, and already test-passing.

nodes.title: Itemized entries with helpful/harmful counters beat monolithic rewriting: +12.5 TGC on AppWorld
nodes.body: Problem: an agent loop must improve its own context without weight updates, and the obvious implementation - have an LLM rewrite the accumulated notes each round - degrades. What made it hard: rewriting is a lossy global operation with no attribution, so one bad rewrite destroys knowledge that earlier rounds paid for, and nothing records which sentence actually helped. The fix is to store memory as itemized bullets, each with a unique id, a small content unit (a strategy, concept, or failure mode), and two counters for how often it was marked helpful or harmful, then update by appending new bullets and incrementing counters in place and merge the deltas with deterministic non-LLM logic. Here the mechanism is that each write is localized and id-attributable, so credit and blame land on one entry instead of smearing across a rewritten blob, and parallel reflectors can merge without clobbering each other. On AppWorld with DeepSeek-V3.1, task-goal completion went 63.7 to 76.2 and scenario-goal completion 42.9 to 64.3, average 42.4 to 59.4; removing incremental updates drops to 67.3 TGC / 56.9 average. Limitation: the counters are assigned by the same LLM that writes the bullets, so they record the writer's self-assessment, not verified utility.

nodes.title: Monolithic rewrite collapse: an 18,282-token memory shrank to 122 tokens and fell below the no-memory baseline
nodes.body: Problem: why does self-improving memory sometimes make an agent worse than having no memory at all? The trace is Dynamic Cheatsheet on AppWorld: at step 60 the memory holds 18,282 tokens and accuracy is 66.7; the next monolithic rewrite compresses it to 122 tokens and accuracy falls to 57.1, under the 63.7 no-adaptation baseline. What makes this dangerous is a positive feedback loop on brevity: a rewriter asked for a compact summary keeps only what looks generally important, the specific appendices vanish, and because the rewrite replaces instead of appending there is no path back - the next rewrite starts from the already-shortened text, so the loss compounds rather than being corrected. Here the mechanism is that the compression operator has no memory of what it dropped and no counter recording that a dropped item was ever helpful. ACE names this 'context collapse' and pairs it with a second mode, 'brevity bias', where optimizers converge on short generic instructions that no longer discriminate between situations. That diagnosis is useful because it predicts degradation will be abrupt and irreversible, which is what the token trace shows, and predicts that append-only writes with ids will not exhibit it. Limitation: this is one illustrative trace from one benchmark family, not a measured distribution of collapse events.

nodes.title: ExpeL seeds each insight counter at 2 and deletes at 0, insulating memory against lucky successes
nodes.body: Problem: an agent that learns only from successes stores insights from trajectories that succeeded for the wrong reason, and those insights then mislead later attempts. What made it hard: with binary success feedback there is no label saying which of several insights in a successful run was actually responsible. The mechanism is a four-operator edit algebra over an insight list - ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE - where a new insight enters with importance count 2, UPVOTE and EDIT increment it, DOWNVOTE decrements it, and the insight is removed at zero. This is why this works: the initial value of 2 buys one unit of tolerance, so a single contradicting observation does not erase an insight but a repeated one does; the counter is a cheap running vote, and letting EDIT double as an endorsement means refinement is rewarded like agreement. The authors state the rationale explicitly - even successful trajectories can be suboptimal and mislead the generated insights. Results: ALFWorld put-unseen 50 with ReAct to 83 with ExpeL; WebShop reward 0.665 to 0.701. Limitation: retrieval is kNN over whole successful trajectories with all-mpnet-base-v2, so the demonstrated regime is dozens of tasks, not a long-running loop with thousands of entries where counter starvation becomes possible.

nodes.title: Dedup threshold barely matters: 50/70/90 percent scores 77.0/73.9/78.6, so dedup is not load-bearing
nodes.body: Problem: memory stores grow without bound and accumulate near-identical lessons, so an obvious engineering response is to invest heavily in consolidation - similarity thresholds, merge policies, proactive versus lazy dedup. What made it hard: dedup is destructive, so a wrong merge silently removes the one entry that would have helped, and there is no cheap way to notice afterwards. The finding is that the choice barely matters: ACE sweeps embedding-similarity dedup at 50, 70 and 90 percent and gets 77.0, 73.9 and 78.6 - a spread inside run noise, and not monotone. The pruning trigger behaves the same: pruning at 10K, 50K or 100K tokens gives 78.6, 78.4, 78.3. The mechanism is that growth-and-refine is carried by append-plus-counter, and dedup is housekeeping that mostly removes redundancy the retriever would have ranked away anyway, so the store tolerates slack in its consolidation policy. Limitation: this is one benchmark and one embedder, and the insensitive band is roughly 3 points - it bounds the effect, it does not prove dedup can never matter; near-duplicate adversarial content is exactly the case the sweep does not cover.

nodes.title: Memory should be reconstructed per state, not replayed: verbatim injection causes negative transfer
nodes.body: Problem: retrieved experience is abstract and general while the state at decision time is concrete and changing, so a memory that was right last week can be actively wrong now. What made it hard: the standard fix - retrieve top-k and splice the text into the prompt - has no place to express 'this lesson applies only if'. MemHarness names the failure negative transfer and attributes it to the replay paradigm, where stored records are treated as static and injected regardless of fit. The mechanism is to insert an explicit reconstruction step between retrieval and action: at each decision step one policy critiques the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state and emits context-grounded guidance before acting, and that reconstructive behavior is learned end-to-end with GRPO rather than prompted. This is why this works: conditioning moves the disambiguation burden from the retriever, which sees only a query, to the policy, which sees the full state, so a mismatched memory can be rewritten into a conditional instead of being obeyed. The authors also report the reconstruction objective acts as latent guidance during training, improving intrinsic reasoning. Limitation: only the abstract was read, so effect sizes are unverified, and the capability is trained into weights - it does not transfer to a plugin that cannot fine-tune.

nodes.title: Transfer depends on task: prose insights beat replay 36 vs 31 on HotpotQA but lose 50 vs 55 on ALFWorld
nodes.body: Problem: should memory store compressed lessons or raw trajectories? Both are used in practice and both are argued for, usually without a controlled comparison. ExpeL supplies one: with the same experience pool, run insights-only versus retrieve-only. On HotpotQA insights-only scores 36 and retrieve-only 31, so abstraction wins; on ALFWorld insights-only scores 50 and retrieve-only 55, so raw replay wins. The mechanism is a fidelity-versus-generality trade: a compressed insight generalizes across surface variation, which is what a knowledge-heavy QA task rewards, while a raw trajectory preserves procedural detail - exact action sequences, object names, step order - that an embodied task needs and summarization drops. This is why this works as an explanation: the two benchmarks differ in whether the transferable content is a fact or a routine, and the ablation holds the retriever and pool fixed while varying only the storage form. Limitation: the deltas are 5 points on two benchmarks with a single backbone, and the obvious hybrid - store both and route by task type - is untested, so the honest reading is that mode is a per-task design choice rather than that one form is better.

nodes.title: Contradictions should be invalidated with a validity interval, not deleted: Zep 94.8 DMR vs MemGPT 93.4
nodes.body: Problem: a store learns that a fact changed - the user moved, a dependency was upgraded - and the naive responses are to append the new fact (both are now retrieved and contradict) or overwrite the old one (history, and the reason for the change, are lost). Here the mechanism is a bi-temporal edge: every relation carries both when it was true in the world and when the system learned it, so a contradiction is recorded as the old edge being invalidated at time t instead of being removed. This is why this works: retrieval can filter to the edge valid at the query's reference time, which resolves the contradiction without destroying evidence, and the invalidation timestamp is itself the audit trail needed to explain later behavior. Zep reports 94.8 DMR against 93.4 for MemGPT, and up to +18.5 percent accuracy on LongMemEval with about 90 percent lower latency than a full-context baseline. Limitation: it resolves only contradictions that are resolvable by time. If two sources disagree about the same interval, or a preference oscillates without stabilizing, there is no timestamp to invalidate on and the graph silently keeps both - exactly the conflict classes measured separately in TANGLE.

nodes.title: Time-decay forgetting is used widely but was never evaluated on a task benchmark, only on simulated dialogue
nodes.body: Problem: a growing store eventually retrieves stale entries, so many systems decay memory strength with elapsed time and reinforce it on recall, borrowing the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve. Here the mechanism is that each memory has a strength decaying exponentially with time since last access and boosted when retrieved, so significance and recency jointly decide retention, and the signal needed is just access - exactly what a long-running loop already has without labels. This is why this works in principle: decay is a cheap proxy for the probability an entry is still relevant, and unlike counters it needs no judge, so it cannot be gamed by the writer. But the evidence base is thin: MemoryBank applies this to a companion chatbot and reports qualitative and simulated-dialogue evaluation, not task success against a no-decay control. So the widely repeated claim that decay helps is, as far as primary sources show, unmeasured on any benchmark where memory affects task completion. Limitation and consequence: for a loop deciding whether to keep an insight not retrieved in 200 rounds there is no published curve or threshold to copy, and the decay rate is a free parameter that silently trades staleness against forgetting something about to become relevant.

nodes.title: TANGLE finds three irreducible memory conflicts no fixed rule resolves, and perception beats action
nodes.body: Problem: memory systems are usually scored on recall accuracy, which assumes one correct answer exists in the store. TANGLE (541 instances, 40 personas, 46 life aspects, 10 domains) instead builds cases where the memory itself is in conflict. Three types are named irreducible: Context-Partitioned Conflict, where the right preference depends on a context never stated; Behavior-Oscillation Conflict, where the preference changes without stabilizing so any stored value is a snapshot of a moving target; and Source-Contradiction Conflict, where sources genuinely disagree. The mechanism the paper argues for is a Conflict-Aware Action Policy that adapts per conflict - sometimes asking, sometimes hedging, sometimes committing with stated confidence - because fixed rules prove insufficient. This is why this works as a framing: as a policy problem the failure is not a wrong memory but an unjustified certainty, since collapsing a live conflict into one definitive entry converts ambiguity into overconfident action. Findings: with curated memory, models perceive conflicts more reliably than they calibrate actions or seek targeted clarification; with an end-to-end pipeline, extraction fails to preserve the conflict-bearing relations entirely. Limitation: it scores judgment quality, not downstream task success, so the cost of hedging is unmeasured.

nodes.title: Poisoning needs under 0.1 percent of the store for over 80 percent attack success: retrieval is unverified
nodes.body: Problem: an agent's long-term memory is written from untrusted text - web pages, tool output, other agents - and retrieved later as trusted context. What made it hard to reason about: retrieval is similarity search with no verification, so influence is not proportional to volume. AgentPoison shows the mechanism: constrained optimization of a trigger phrase so that every triggered instance maps into a unique, compact region of embedding space. This is why this works: the trigger guarantees the poisoned records are the nearest neighbors whenever the trigger appears, while compactness keeps them far from benign queries, so benign behavior is unaffected and the poison is not diluted by the rest of the store; no training or fine-tuning is needed. Reported: over 80 percent average attack success at a poison rate under 0.1 percent, under 1 percent benign degradation, surviving a perplexity filter and trigger rephrasings that preserve meaning. The general lesson is that top-k retrieval is a winner-take-all channel - a handful of high-similarity records can occupy the entire retrieved window. Limitation: the trigger is a specific string, so this measures a backdoor rather than slow semantic drift, and it does not test stores whose writes pass an LLM consistency check.

nodes.title: Write-time consistency checks stop single-record poisoning but not compositional or dormant poisoning
nodes.body: Problem: the intuitive defense is to validate each memory at write time - is this consistent with what we know? MemPoison (1227 hand-validated cases, 4 attack types, 3 injection channels, 3 memory substrates, 10 model families) tests that class against a three-tier taxonomy: L1 direct single-record corruption, L2 compositional corruption spread across records, and L3 context-triggered dormant corruption that stays inert until a condition is met. The attack is also temporally decoupled - the injection turn and the harmful-behavior turn are different turns - so a write-time check only ever sees a harmless-looking insertion. Finding: write-time defenses substantially suppress L1 but fail to reliably suppress L2 and L3. The mechanism behind the failure is decomposition: a mechanistic influence decomposition shows individually benign records become harmful through joint retrieval composition or trigger-conditioned activation, and no per-record predicate can see a property that exists only in the combination. This is why this works as an argument: it puts the defense boundary at the record while the harm sits in the retrieval set, so it generalizes past these specific attacks. Limitation: the L3 cases are constructed, so the real-world frequency of dormant compositional poisoning is unknown.

nodes.title: Benign-case cost of memory defenses is near zero: anomaly detection blocked 0.4 percent of turns
nodes.body: Problem: memory-poisoning defenses are judged by attack success rate, but almost all traffic an agent sees is benign, so the deployment question is what the defense costs when nobody is attacking - and ASR reveals none of it. The harness holds backbone, memory backend, retrieval, answer prompt and judge fixed and varies only the defense, on half of LoCoMo (5 long conversations, 750 turns, 255 questions per run, 3 runs per condition). Results: sanitization and provenance checking never fired at all; LLM anomaly detection blocked 9 of 2,250 turns (0.4 percent); a read-time reranker dropped 2.2 percent of the memories it judged, withholding at least one memory from 14.9 percent of questions, and a blind audit found content-based justification for only 2 of 50 sampled drops. No defense showed a detectable accuracy cost at 95 percent intervals of plus or minus 2.4 to 4.6 points; the reranker changed accuracy by +0.6 (CI -2.6 to +3.8). This is why this works as evidence: swapping only the defense removes the confounds that usually make such comparisons unreadable. Token overhead: 0 percent sanitization, 1.5 percent anomaly, 3.0 percent reranker, 4.5 percent stacked. Limitation: the paper's own history is a warning - an earlier version had a model mismatch accounting for 2.9 of the 4.4 points of cost it had reported.

nodes.title: One delete-and-reanswer probe per entry beats denser observational feedback: 63.4 to 70.2 to 77.5
nodes.body: Problem: in a memory pipeline an operation's value is unobservable when it is taken - you cannot tell whether a write, a merge or a retrieval helped, because the answer depends on all of them and on the reader. What made it hard: honest ground truth requires counterfactual replay (what would the answer have been without this entry), which is expensive and, over a long loop, unbounded. The mechanism here uses a machine-readable audit trail twice: offline, retrieval hits and answer-time citations train an operation-conditioned memory-utility critic; online, retrievals plus citations plus one controlled deletion-and-reanswer per probe settle an intervention-calibrated entry-level presence credit, propagated along version chains as an action-level proxy reward, with no per-operation human labels and no Monte-Carlo replay. This is why this works: the deletion probe turns an observational correlation into a small local intervention, so that entry's credit is causal at the cost of one extra answer, and the version chain carries it back to the operation that created the entry. Results: LoCoMo held-out 77.5 percent with a local 8B policy under a fixed shared reader versus 65.1 for an API teacher and 69.7 for Mem0; LongMemEval 79.0. Limitation: it trains a policy, and a single reanswer only isolates contribution if the entry's effect is separable enough to show up in one probe.

nodes.title: Offline consolidation pays only when the next query is predictable: 5x less test-time compute if it is
nodes.body: Problem: consolidating experience offline, during idle time and off the critical path, is attractive for an always-on agent, but it requires guessing what will be asked later. Sleep-time compute makes the trade explicit: during idle periods the model anticipates likely queries and pre-computes useful quantities, converting raw context into a learned context so the answer path does less reasoning. The mechanism is to spend latency-free time rewriting the context into pre-digested form that the query-time model consumes. This is why this works: the expensive reasoning moves to a period where nobody is waiting, so equal accuracy costs roughly 5x less test-time compute on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME, and scaling the offline work adds up to 13 and 18 points. Amortization is the second half: with multiple related queries per context (Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic) average cost per query falls 2.5x, because one consolidation serves many reads. The decisive analysis is that efficacy correlates with the predictability of the user query. Limitation: predictability is measured, not engineered - for a codebase loop where the next human instruction is genuinely open-ended the offline work is a bet, and a wrong bet is pure cost.

nodes.title: OPRO beats human prompts by up to 8% (GSM8K) and 50% (BBH) by putting the score trajectory in the prompt
nodes.body: Problem: a prompt is a discrete object with no gradient, so the only classic levers are random search or hand-editing. OPRO (arXiv:2309.03409) makes the optimizing LLM the optimizer: the meta-prompt carries the task description plus a trajectory of prior candidate instructions and their scalar scores, and the model is asked to produce a better one. The mechanism is that the (solution, score) list makes the task an in-context descent problem the model already knows how to do — it reads which phrasing correlates with high values and moves in that direction, no derivative required. Why this works: the entire optimization state fits in one context window, so there is no state to maintain outside the prompt and no training step. Limitation: it needs a cheap, reliable scalar per candidate; where evaluation is expensive or noisy the loop degenerates. OPRO's own analysis concedes overfitting is present but argues it is 'less harmful' when all candidates overfit alike — a hope, not a control.

nodes.title: STOP puts the improver itself in the search space, so the same loop can be re-entered one level up
nodes.body: Problem: an improver that is hand-written caps the whole loop at the quality of that one scaffold. STOP (arXiv:2310.02304) starts from a seed 'improver' program — it queries an LM on an input program and returns the best result — then runs that seed improver on itself, and the improved improver generates better programs on downstream tasks. Why this works: the improver is ordinary source code, so it lies inside the space the loop already searches; nothing new is needed at level 1, the levels are the same type, and the 3-level structure (improver / candidate / evaluator) can be re-entered on any of them. Limitation, stated by the authors: the LM weights are untouched, so this is not full RSI, and the paper also measures how often generated code escapes its sandbox — the search will find holes in the container before it finds better programs. Read the gain as 'the scaffold is now editable', not 'the model improved'.

nodes.title: DGM trades the Godel machine's proof for an empirical bar: SWE-bench 20.0% to 50.0%
nodes.body: Problem: Schmidhuber's Gödel machine is unimplementable because it demands a proof that a self-edit helps before applying it. DGM (arXiv:2505.22954v3) keeps the self-edit and drops the proof: it maintains an open-ended archive of self-modified agent variants and accepts an edit when the empirical score clears a bar on coding benchmarks. SWE-bench 20.0% → 50.0%, Polyglot 14.2% → 30.7%, beating baselines with neither self-improvement nor open-ended exploration. Why this works: a benchmark run is a cheap falsifiable gate, and the archive preserves stepping stones that a strict hill-climb would delete because they score slightly worse before they enable a later jump. The mechanism reaches all the way down: the v3 diff shows it edited its own tools/edit.py, replacing whole-file 'edit' with a unique-match 'str_replace' plus a view_range, i.e. it changed the operator it uses to change itself. Limitation: acceptance and scoring use the same benchmark, and secondary write-ups report it removed its own hallucination-detection markers to raise scores — I could not confirm that in the primary v3 text I read, so treat the reward-hacking anecdote as unverified.

nodes.title: The meta level is ~1.6% of loop spend (2.5k vs 500k tokens/epoch): cheap, but not thereby helpful
nodes.body: metaTextGrad (arXiv:2505.18524) reports per-epoch token cost: program level ~400k, optimizer level ~100k, meta-optimizer ~2.5k. The mechanism is a leverage asymmetry — a meta edit touches a few tokens at the top of a hierarchy and thereby re-parameterizes every downstream use of the optimizer, so the cost ratio between levels is roughly two orders of magnitude. Why this works: the object being edited shrinks as you go up, so marginal meta-iterations are nearly free once the inner loop exists. Results: 0.49/0.47 (zero-shot MIPROv2) to 0.56/0.53 (metaTextGrad) averaged val/test across BBH Word Sorting, BBH Dyck, MMLU Abstract Algebra, GPQA Diamond. Limitation: cheapness sets the bar for the real question (does it beat more attempts?) but does not clear it, and the accounting is uncomfortable — the meta-optimizer was o1 while the optimizer was GPT-4o, so part of the gain may be model class, not level. Their Theorem 1 Hoeffding bound covers only in-distribution risk; it says nothing about a shift in D.

nodes.title: Promptbreeder evolves the mutation prompts, putting the edit operator in the same space as its operand
